# About the Data and Case Study

In this Case Study, we will examine the \verb|Credit| dataset from ISLR
R package. This dataset has a lot of predictors, some of which are
categorical (factor), and is a perfect illustration of feature selection
by stepwise selection and regularization.

You may have already seen the Credit data when taking other courses, but
our treatment here will have a much heavier Data Mining flavor and will
be structured in a way that you will be working on each step of Model
Building Process on this realistic dataset.

This *Case Study* is to identify and interpret key factors that relate
to a higher or lower Balance with the aid of appropriate linear models.
The scope of this *Case Study* is strictly to illustrate the fundamental
tools of *Data Mining* and for *Linear Models*. The linear model
considered is \begin{align}
\label{eqn:MLR1}
Y 
& = 
\beta_{0} 
+ 
\beta_{1} X_{1} 
+ 
\beta_{2} X_{2} 
+ 
\cdots 
+ 
\beta_{p} X_{p} 
+ 
\epsilon. 
\end{align}

First of all, let's first read in the dataset, delete the first column
containing row only indices, and print a summary of each variable.

```{r}
# Uncomment the next line the first time you use ISLR
# install.packages("ISLR")
library(ISLR)
data(Credit)

# Delete the first column containing row indices
Credit$ID <- NULL

summary(Credit)
```

The dataset should have $n = 400$ observations and 11 variables. To know
about the variables, run the fullowing line.

```{r}
help(Credit)
dim(Credit)
names(Credit)
```

Numeric predictors are listed first, followed by categorical ones. The
target variable is the last variable in the dataset, \verb|Balance|, an
integer-valued variable that ranges from O to 1,999 and represents the
credit card balance (in\$) for an individual. The other variables
describe the financial and demographic factors of an individual and can
be grouped as follows:

- The first six variables, \verb|Income|, \verb|Limit|, \verb|Rating|,
  \verb|Cards|, \verb|Age|, and \verb|Education|, are numeric predictors
  for \verb|Balance|.

- The other four variables, \verb|Gender|, \verb|Student|,
  \verb|Married|, and \verb|Ethnicity|, are categorical predictors. The
  first three variables are binary and \verb|Ethnicity| has three
  levels.

# Exercise 1

Is there any variable with ethical concerns?

Well, \verb|Ethnicity| variable could be of potential concern which
could raise the issues of discrimination and legal concerns.

# Exercise 2

In this exercise, let's do some EDA.

## Target Variable

How does the distribution of target variable look like? Based on your
observation, what transformation would be suitable for Balance in order
to fit a linear model? Remember that for linear regression model, the
target variable should be approximately normally distributed.

```{r}
summary(Credit$Balance)

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(Credit , aes(x = Balance)) +
  geom_histogram()

nrow(Credit [Credit$Balance == 0, ])
```

We observed that the median, mean, and maximum of Balance are 459.50,
520.01, and 1,999, respectively. Since mean exceeds the median, then the
distribution of Balance is skewed to the right (although the skewness
does not seem severe). This is also confirmed by the histogram of
Balance provided.

Since the distribution is positively skewed, it would be ideal to use
log-transformation to the data. However, there are a large number of
observations (90 to be exact) for which Balance equals zero. This makes
the log-transformation problematic and so we will leave Balance as is.
Given the log-transformation is not suitable, the other possible
skewness correction transformation would be to use the square-root
transformation.

```{r}
ggplot(Credit , aes(x = sqrt(Balance))) +
  geom_histogram()
```

## Investigating Numeric Predictors -- Bivariate Data Exploration

Report the correlation matrix of the numeric predictors.

```{r}
# Calculate the correlation matrix for numeric variables
# The numeric predictors are in the first 6 columns
cor.matrix <- cor(Credit[, c(1:6, 11)])
print("Correlation Matrix")
round(cor.matrix, digits = 4)
```

- Predictive Variables of Balance: Limit and Rating with high
  correlation to Balance. Income variable has moderate effect with
  Balance. The rest of the numeric variables, e.g., Age, Education,
  etc., have very weak effect on the target variable, Balance.

- Correlations Between Predictors: Note the following correlations.

  - Between Income and Limit (0.7921)
  - Between Income and Rating (0.7914)
  - Between Limit and Rating (0.9969)

These large correlations can be of concern as they suggest duplication
of information contained in the three variables and may complicate the
interpretation of the regression coefficients. The last correlation is
most alarming, indicating that Limit and Rating are almost positively
collinear.

```{r}
ggplot(Credit, aes(x = Limit, y = Rating)) + 
  geom_point()
```

The scatterplot above reveals that the two variables (Limit and Rating)
are virtually perfectly related in a linear fashion and do not
contribute much information when the other variable is present.
Therefore, we will keep one and only one of the two predictors, say
Rating, and delete Limit. This can be justified by the slightly higher
correlation between Rating and Balance as seen in the correlation matrix
above.

```{r}
# Delete Limit
Credit$Limit <- NULL
```

## Visualization

Create visual representations between the numeric variables and the
target variable to identify variables most likely to predict the target.

Scatterplots between numeric variables and target variable is shown
below.

```{r}
# first save the names of the numeric predictors as a vector
vars.numeric <- colnames(Credit[, 1:5])
for (i in vars.numeric) {
  plot <- ggplot(Credit, aes(x = Credit[, i], y = Balance)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
    labs(x = i)
  print(plot)
}
```

# Exercise 3

Here we explore the factor variables. Identify a factor variable that is
more likely to predict the target variable.

- Show key descriptive statistics.
- Create visual representations (e.g., graphs, charts).
- Explain why you selected this variable and how the variable relates to
  the target variable.

Well, there are four categorical predictors,
\verb|Gender, Student, Married|, and \verb|Ethnicity|, and identify one
of them which is likely to be predictive. Some preliminary descriptive
statistics of these four variables can be found in the summary in
Exercise 1. For instance, 360 (90%) of the observations are non-students
while 40 (10%) of them are students.

Let's produce the mean (and median) of \verb|Balance| split by different
levels of each of the four factor variables.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

# Save the names of the categorical predictors as a vector!
vars.categorical <- c("Gender", "Student", "Married", "Ethnicity")
for (i in vars.categorical) {
  x <- Credit %>%
    group_by_(i) %>%
    summarise(
      mean = mean(Balance),
      median = median(Balance),
      n = n()
      )
  print(x)
}
```

Of the four categorical predictors, only Student stands out as making a
significant difference to the mean of Balance over the two levels, "Yes"
and "No", with students (876.8250) having a much higher average Balance
than for non-students (480.3694). The mean of Balance is more or less
the same across different levels of Gender, Married, and Ethnicity.
These three variables appear to be ineffective in differentiating the
observations of Balance.

Let's supplement our conclusions above with some graphical displays,
Split Boxplots. Since Balance is a numeric variable but we are now
dealing with categorical predictors, we will make use of split boxplots.

```{r}
for (i in vars.categorical) {
  plot <- ggplot(Credit, aes(x = Credit[, i], y = Balance)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    labs(x = i)
  print(plot)
}
```

As we expect, the box for students is noticeably higher than that for
non-students, with a similar spread, and the boxes are very similar
across different factor levels for each of Gender, Married, and
Ethnicity. These observations support our earlier findings that Student
seems to be the only factor variable with significant predictive power.

**Conclusion:** Overall, the most promising predictors for Balance are
Income (numeric), Rating (numeric), and Student (factor).

# Exercise 4

Comment about the following two plots. Clearly state your observations
and discuss the impact, if any, of each plot on your later modeling.

## A Boxplot of Age by Student

```{r}
ggplot(Credit, aes(x = Student, y = Age)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

The plot above shows that those who are students tend to have a smaller
Age (a lower median). This makes intuitive sense as students are more
likely to be younger, although the median Age of students, which is
close to 50, seems unreasonably high (well, this dataset is simulated!).
However, this also means that there is some co-dependence (but not
interaction!) between Age and Student, and the effects of these two
variables on Balance may be distorted when they serve as predictors at
the same time. Fortunately, this concern may not be relevant after all,
as we have seen in Exercise 2 that Age is unlikely to be an important
predictor of Balance.

## A Scatterplot of Balance against Income colored by Student

A scatterplot of Balance against Income with the observations colored by
Student and with a smoothed line superimposed for each level of Student
can be created as below. This plot highlights the possible interaction
between Income and Student in affecting Balance. How?

```{r}
ggplot(Credit, aes(x = Income, y = Balance, color = Student)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

Recall that an interaction means that the expected effect of one
predictor on the target variable depends on the value or level of
another predictor. This is reflected in the scatterplot, where the
slopes of the two smoothed lines differ quite remarkably, with the
non-students being more sensitive to Income than students perhaps due to
their financial status. To accommodate the interaction between Income
and Student, we will include the interaction variable Income: Student
when constructing linear models in later exercises.

# Exercise 5

## Split the data into training and test sets

By using \verb|createDataPartition()| function, create the training and
testing split.

```{r}
library(caret)
set.seed(8964)
partition <- createDataPartition(Credit$Balance, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
data.train <- Credit[partition, ]
data.test <- Credit[-partition, ]

print("data.train")
mean(data.train$Balance)

print("data.test")
mean(data.test$Balance)
```

As seen above, the mean of Balance in the training set is pretty close
to that in the test set due to the built-in stratification.

## Fitting MLR

Now, we fit a multiple linear regression model for Balance on all
variables (except Limit) on the training set. Be sure to take note of
the implications in Exercise 4. Interpret the coefficient estimates for
Married and for the Asian level of Ethnicity.

```{r}
model.full <- lm(Balance ~ . + Income:Student, data = data.train)
summary(model.full)
```

The coefficient estimates for the categorical predictors have to be
interpreted differently from those for numeric predictors. Taking the
estimates for MarriedYes and EthnicityAsian for illustration, we can
say:

- The credit card balance of married individuals is lower than that of
  unmarried (baseline) by 20.46469 on average, holding all other
  predictors fixed.

- The credit card balance of Asians is higher than that of African
  Americans (baseline) by 6.53269 on average, holding all other
  predictors fixed.

## Relevel the Factor Variables

Relevel the factor variables so that the most frequent level becomes the
baseline level (more common practice!) and refit the multiple linear
regression model. Interpret the coefficient estimates for Married and
for the Asian level of Ethnicity again.

```{r}
for (i in vars.categorical){
  # Use the table() function to calculate the frequencies for each factor
  table <- as.data.frame(table(Credit[, i]))
  # Determine the level with the highest frequency
  max <- which.max(table[, 2])
  # Save the name of the level with the highest frequency
  level.name <- as.character(table[max, 1])
  # Set the baseline level to the most populous level
  Credit[, i] <- relevel(Credit[, i], ref = level.name)
}

print("Dimension of the dataset Credit!")
dim(Credit)

print("Summary Statistics!")
summary(Credit[, vars.categorical])
```

While releveling has no effect on the predicted values of the linear
model, changing the baseline levels will affect the coefficient
estimates of the dummy variables (which are now dummy variables with
respect to another baseline level) and possibly the significance
statistics such as $t$-statistics for the dummy variables and the
corresponding $p$-values. Remember, the $p$-values measure how different
the non-baseline levels are from the baseline level, and changing the
baseline level certainly changes the measurement of such differences.

As you can see, the baseline levels of Gender, Married, and Ethnicity
have been changed respectively from "Male", "No", and "African American"
to "Female", ""Yes''"Yes", and "Caucasian", which now come first in the
frequency tables for Married and Ethnicity.

Let's refine the model fitted above with releveling.

```{r}
# To make sure factors in the training set are releveled
data.train <- Credit[partition, ]

model.full <- lm(Balance ~ . + Income:Student, data = data.train)
summary(model.full)
```

# Exercise 6 -- Manual Binarization of Factor Variables

## Advantages and Disadvantages of Binarizing the Factor Variables

Describe the advantages and disadvantages of binarizing the factor
variables before performing feature selection.

Before implementing feature selection, sometimes it is desirable to
explicitly binarize categorical predictors with three or more levels.
Although the \verb|lm()| function is capable of automatically converting
categorical predictors into dummy variables behind the scenes, as we
observed before, and so whether or not we binarize the categorical
predictors in advance has no impact on a fitted linear model, explicitly
doing binarization can help make the feature selection process we are
going to perform more meaningful.

Well, then how to binarize a factor variables in R?

Compared to generating new features such as $x^2$, $x^3$, $\log(x)$,
etc., for a numeric variable $x$, binarization of categorical variables
is conceptually more subtle and programmatically more difficult to
implement in R. One of the common functions to be used is the
\verb|dummyVars()| function in t e caret package and we will use it.
Among the four categorical variables Gender, Student, Married, and
Ethnicity, only Ethnicity has more than two levels and has to be
binarized by two dummy variables.

```{r}
library(caret)
binarizer <- dummyVars(paste("~", paste(vars.categorical, collapse = "+")),
                       data = Credit, fullRank = TRUE)
# OR type out the categorical predictors one by one
# binarizer <- dummyVars(~ Gender + Student + Married + Ethnicity,
#                       data = Credit, fullRank = TRUE)
binarized_vars <- data.frame(predict(binarizer, newdata = Credit))
head(binarized_vars)
```

The \verb|binarized_vars| data frame contains all of the dummy
variables. So, let's combine it with the original Credit dataset via the
\verb|cbind()| function and rename it with a \verb|.bin| suffix to
distinguish it from the original non-binarized dataset.

```{r}
Credit.bin <- cbind(Credit, binarized_vars)
head(Credit.bin)
```

Given the binarized variables, the original categorical predictors are
no longer needed as they duplicate the information contained in the
dummy variables. They can be dropped by assigning them to the
\verb|NULL| symbol.

```{r}
Credit.bin$Gender <- NULL
Credit.bin$Student <- NULL
Credit.bin$Married <- NULL
Credit.bin$Ethnicity <- NULL
head(Credit.bin)
```

Now that the expanded dataset with binarized variables is available, we
again split it into the training and test sets.

```{r}
data.train.bin <- Credit.bin[partition, ]
data.test.bin <- Credit.bin[-partition, ]
```

## Refitting the MLR with Binarization

Regardless, binarize the factor variables and refit the multiple linear
regression model in Exercise 5.

```{r}
# The interaction term is now Income:Student.Yes, not Income:Student
model.full.bin <- lm(Balance ~ . + Income:Student.Yes, data = data.train.bin)
summary(model.full.bin)
```

# Exercise 7 -- Feature Selection

Of course, some of the features in the full model may lack predictive
power and result in overfitting.

## Stepwise Selection

Perform stepwise selection using the \verb|stepAIC()| function to
determine which features should be retained.

- When using this function, there are two decisions to make:

  - Forward (direction = "forward") vs. backward (direction =
    "backward").
  - AIC (k = 2) vs. BIC (k = log(nrow(data.train))).

  Describe each decision and the implications in choosing one option
  versus the other.

- Employ forward selection using BIC.

## Backward Selection with the AIC

Run the summary function on the linear model selected by this process.
Provide the summary output and list the variables selected.

```{r}
# install.packages("MASS")  
# uncomment this line the first time you use MASS

library(MASS)
model.backward.AIC <- stepAIC(model.full.bin)

print("Model Summary!")
summary(model.backward.AIC)
```

The following six features remain in the fin al model:

- Income
- Rating
- Age
- Gender.Female
- Student.Yes
- Married.Yes

## Stepwise Selection for Non-binarized Data

If we perform backward stepwise selection for the linear model fitted to
the non-binarized training set. Pay attention to the Ethnicity variable.

```{r}
model.no.binarize <- stepAIC(model.full, steps = 1)
```

Without binarization, the entire Ethnicity variable, which is associated
with two degrees of freedom (look at the Df column), one for each of the
two non-baseline levels, is treated as a single predictor and considered
being dropped altogether. Although this does not make a material
difference in this case study, in other cases t his may not be desirable
as we are ignoring the possibility that only one of the two non-baseline
levels of Ethnicity is insignificant while the other one is significant
(with respect to the baseline).

## Forward Selection with the BIC

To perform forward selection requires more coding effort. Besides the
additional option \verb|direction = "forward"| to mean that we are doing
forward selection, we have to specify, in the scope argument of the
\verb|stepAIC()| function, a two-component list to define the range of
models to be examined in the stepwise selection process.

```{r}
# first fit the null model (i.e., model with no predictors)
model.null <- lm(Balance ~ 1, data = data.train.bin)

model.forward.BIC <- stepAIC(model.null,
                             direction = "forward",
                             scope = list(upper = model.full.bin,
                                          lower = model.null),
                             k = log(nrow(data.train.bin)))

print("Model Summary!")
summary(model.forward.BIC)
```

Features are added in the following order:

- Rating
- Income
- Student.No

# Exercise 8 -- Model Validation

Here we select and validate the recommended model.

Now that we have different linear models of varying degrees of
complexity fitted to the training set, it is time to compare their
predictive performance on the common test set and see which one is the
most predictive. We are particularly interested in whether reducing the
complexity of a linear model by stepwise selection algorithms can
enhance prediction accuracy.

## Computing RMSEs

Evaluate the RMSE of the models in the preceding exercises against the
test set.

A natural and direct measure of the prediction performance of linear
models, where the target variable is numeric, is the test RMSE. The
smaller the test RMSE, the better. Here, we compute and prints the test
RMSE of the four models we have constructed.

```{r}
RMSE(data.test$Balance, predict(model.null, newdata = data.test.bin))
RMSE(data.test$Balance, predict(model.full.bin, newdata = data.test.bin))
RMSE(data.test$Balance, predict(model.backward.AIC, newdata = data.test.bin))
RMSE(data.test$Balance, predict(model.forward.BIC, newdata = data.test.bin))
```

For your convenience, the following table reports the test RMSE
extracted from the R output for each of the four models.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("MLR_Credit_RMSEs1.png")
```

## Recommendation

Make a recommendation as to which model should be used.

Observe that the two reduced models resulting from stepwise selection
have a (slightly) lower test RMSE than the full model despite having far
fewer features. Comparing the two reduced models, we can see that the
model based on forward selection and BIC not only is simpler in the
sense that it is nested within that based on the backward selection and
AIC, but also is more predictive in the sense that its test RMSE is
lower. On the basis of both prediction accuracy and interpretability,
the final model based on forward selection and BIC is justifiably the
most promising model among all of the linear models we have considered
and we will recommend using this model.

## Model Diagnostic

Generate and interpret diagnostic plots for the recommended model to
check the model assumptions.

Now that the model based on forward selection and BIC appears to be the
best among the four linear models, let's diagnose it carefully for any
anomalies with the use of appropriate graphical displays.

```{r}
plot(model.forward.BIC)
```

# Exercise 9 -- Regularization -- Important

Elastic net (ET) could also be used to perform feature selection.

```{r}
# This is externally typed LaTeX content. 
knitr::include_graphics("ET_Reg1.png")
```

An alternative to using stepwise selection for identifying useful
features is regularization, which reduces the magnitude of the
coefficient estimates via the use of a penalty term and serves to
prevent overfitting. Variables with limited predictive power will
receive a coefficient estimate that is small, if not exactly zero, and
therefore are removed from the model. In this exercise, we will fit a
regularized regression model with alpha equal to 0.5 (i.e., an even mix
between ridge regression and lasso) to the Credit dataset and compare
its performance to that of the models based on the stepwise selection.
Because our goal in this case study is to identify key factors affecting
Balance, using alpha equal to 0, which is ridge regression and does not
eliminate any variables, is not appropriate.

## The glmnet() Function

To implement regularization, we will use the \verb|glmnet| package,
where the main function is the \verb|glmnet()| function.

This function can be used to fit ridge regression models, lasso models,
and general elastic nets, but it has different syntax from the
\verb|lm()| function you have been familiar with. You have to supply the
design matrix as input via \verb|model.matrix()| function.

```{r}
X.train <- model.matrix(Balance ~ . + Income:Student, data = data.train)
head(X.train)  # print out a few rows of the design matrix
```

A particular advantage of the \verb|model.matrix()| function is that
categorical predictors will be automatically transformed into dummy
variables, just like the \verb|dummyVars()| function, and the design
matrix is of full rank.

As soon as a design matrix has been set up, it can be passed to the
\verb|glmnet()| function along withthe vector of response values and the
values of the hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\lambda$.

## Fitting Elastic Net (ET)

Now, we fit five regularized regression models with $\alpha =0.5$ and
$\lambda = 0, 10, 100, 500, 1000$ (one model for each value of$\lambda$)
to the training set, and save the five fitted models collectively as an
object named \verb|m.lambda|. Note that the family argument is set to
"gaussian" because we are dealing with linear models with normal (a.k.a.
Gaussian) errors.

```{r}
#install.packages("glmnet")  
# uncomment this line the first time you use glmnet
library(glmnet)
m.lambda <- glmnet(x = X.train,
                   y = data.train$Balance,
                   family = "gaussian",
                   lambda = c(0, 10, 100, 500, 1000),
                   alpha = 0.5)
```

The first way to extract coefficient estimates is as given below:

```         
m.lambda$a0
m.lambda$beta
```

The second way extract the estimated coefficients is to use
\verb|coef()| function to a \verb|glmnet| object returns a matrix of
coefficient estimates, including the intercept, arranged by columns
according to different values of $\lambda$.

```{r}
round(coef(m.lambda), 4)
```

When $\lambda = 1,000$, the regularization penalty is so large that all
of the coefficient estimates except the intercept become exactly zero,
in which case the model is effectively the null model with only the
intercept. The estimated intercept should be the mean value of Balance
in the training set.

```{r}
mean(data.train$Balance)
```

# Exercise 10 -- Cross-Validation -- Important

This exercise is specifically to learn the process of **Hyperparameter
Tuning**, an important concept in ML.

## cv.glmnet() Function

The \verb|glmnet()| function requires that value(s) $\lambda$ be
supplied a priori and does not directly tell us the optimal value of
$\lambda$. In fact, in Exercise 9 we experimented with five
pre-specified values of $\lambda$, mainly to explore the impact of
regularization but did not attempt to optimize the value of $\lambda$.
Fortunately, the companion function \verb|cv.glmnet()| (with "cv"
standing for Cross Validation) fills this gap. This function performs
$k$-fold cross-validation (10-fold cross-validation, by default),
calculates the cross-validation error for a range of values of
$\lambda$, and produces the optimal value of $\lambda$ as a by-product.

You may supply a sequence of values of $\lambda$ to be tested or the
\verb|cv.glmnet()| will choose the values of $\lambda$ in its own. The
default value is NULL.

The \verb|cv.glmnet()| function is commonly accompanied with an
application of the \verb|plot()| function to a \verb|cv.glmnet()|
object. This returns a cross-validation curve, that is, the
cross-validation error plotted as a function of the values of $\lambda$
used. Such a plot has several useful features:

```{r}
# This is externally typed LaTeX content. 
knitr::include_graphics("CV_Features1.png")
```

## Tuning Hyperparameter via CV

Use cross-validation to set the value of $\lambda$ for fitting the
regularized model ($\alpha = 0.5$) in Exercise 9.

- List the features used in the resulting model. Compare the selected
  features to those using stepwise regression in Exercise 7. Comment on
  any differences.

- Calculate the RMSE on the test set.

\*\* Recommend which model should be used. Justify your choice.

```{r}
set.seed(1111)
m <- cv.glmnet(x = X.train,
               y = data.train$Balance,
               family = "gaussian",
               nfold = 10,
               #lambda = NULL, 
               lambda = 1:20,
               alpha = 0.5)
plot(m)

m$lambda.min
m$lambda.1se
```

We now refit the regularized model on the training set with
$\lambda = 0.8885539$, save it as an object named \\verb\|m.min\$, make
predictions on the test set, and finally evaluate the model's RMSE.

```{r}
# Fit the regularized model using lambda.min
m.min <- glmnet(x = X.train,
                y = data.train$Balance,
                family = "gaussian",
                lambda = m$lambda.min,
                alpha = 0.5)

# List the coefficient estimates
m.min$beta

# Set up the design matrix for the test set
X.test <- model.matrix(Balance ~ . + Income:Student, data = data.test)

# Make predictions on the test set and calculate test RMSE
m.min.pred <- predict(m.min, newx = X.test)
RMSE(data.test$Balance, m.min.pred)
```

**Conclusion:** The test RMSE of the resulting model is 103.9201, which
is slightly higher than that of the final model in exercise 7 (which is
102.6785). In addition to inferior predictive performance, the
regularized model is also much harder to interpret due to its
substantially larger size, whereas the model in exercise 7 only has
three features. As a result, it is reasonable to recommend the model in
Exercise 7 as the final model owing to its better prediction accuracy
and interpretability.

## Other than CV for Tuining?

Suggest another method to set the value of lambda. There is no need to
implement this method.

This is exactly asking "Fitting the Regularized Model With lambda.1se."

Instead of using the value of $\lambda$ that minimizes the
cross-validation error, we can also select $\lambda$ based on the
one-standard-error rule and set it equal to \verb|lambda.1se|, or
7.550517 (which is much larger than \verb|lambda.min|).

```{r}
# Fit the regularized model using lambda.1se
m.1se <- glmnet(x = X.train,
                y = data.train$Balance,
                family = "gaussian",
                lambda = m$lambda.1se,
                alpha = 0.5)

# List the coefficient estimates
m.1se$beta

# Make predictions on the test set and calculate test RMSE
m.1se.pred <- predict(m.1se, newx = X.test)
RMSE(data.test$Balance, m.1se.pred)
```
